idiom_name: opaque struct plus constructor/method functions (hand-rolled vtable for polymorphism)
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the whole structure is hand-written: declare the type opaquely in the header (typedef struct Order Order;) and keep the struct definition in the .c file so callers cannot touch the fields; build instances through an Order_create-style constructor that establishes every invariant, expose behaviour as functions taking the object first (bool order_add_line(Order *, const Line *, OrderError **)), and give each type a matching _destroy. Polymorphic domain families need a struct of function pointers - the vtable idiom used by Samek's OOP-in-C and QP frameworks - or GObject, which supplies a type system, class structs and signals at the cost of adopting GLib; the source article notes that OOP in C is otherwise cumbersome and error prone. Persistence stays in a separate module that maps rows to and from the domain structs; the struct itself never knows about it.
pitfalls: The header convention is the only encapsulation: if the struct definition leaks into a public header, any code can corrupt the state - keep it in the .c file or a private header.
Every _create needs a matching _destroy, and nested domain objects need a documented ownership rule (or an arena/region allocator), otherwise long-lived models leak.
Returning internal pointers (for example the line array) hands out mutable state; return copies or const views.
